label: eq:Silverman-ell-f
title: Remark
body_md:
In codimension one, \cref{cor:no-intermediate-growth} gives a negative answer to Hasselblatt--Propp's intermediate-growth question for dominant rational maps \cite[Question~9.5]{HP07}; see also its precursor \cite[\S5]{BV99}.
For a dominant rational self-map $f$ of $\mathbb{P}^d$, Silverman \cite[Conjecture~2]{Silverman14} conjectured that the quantity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Silverman-ell-f}
\ell_f \coloneqq \inf\biggl\{\ell\geq0:\sup_{n\geq1} \frac{\deg_{1,\mathscr{O}(1)}(f^n)}{n^\ell \lambda_1(f)^n}<\infty\biggr\}
\end{equation}
exists and is an integer with $0\leq \ell_f\leq d$.
For $X=\mathbb{P}^d$ and $i=1$, the estimate \eqref{eq:global-polynomial-growth} proves that $\ell_f$ is finite and at most $2(d-1)$, but it does not assert integrality.
Cantat observed that $\ell_f$ can already equal $4$ in dimension three through the Oguiso--Truong quotient construction \cite{OT15}; see \cite[Example~1.11]{Urech18}.
The same estimate \eqref{eq:global-polynomial-growth} proves the polynomial-upper-bound part of Cantat's question for birational maps with $\lambda_1(f)=1$ \cite[Question~3.2]{Cantat18-ICM}, but it does not establish the additional alternative that every unbounded degree sequence grows at least linearly.
                                                                                          
Finally, \eqref{eq:global-log-growth} affirmatively answers \cite[Question~11]{Silverman26} and establishes its higher-codimensional and K\"ahler analogues.
We refer to \cref{question:polynomial-dyn-deg,rmk:polynomial-dyn-deg-known} for a further discussion.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
As another consequence of \cref{thm:affine-interval-growth}, we obtain an explicit exponential-polynomial upper bound for the volume of the iterated graph $\Gamma_{[n]}$:
\[
\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})=O\bigl(n^{(d^3+2d)/3}\Lambda(f)^n\bigr),\qquad \Lambda(f)\coloneqq\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\lambda_i(f),
\]
which refines Dinh--Sibony's volume estimate $\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})\leq C_\epsilon\, n^d(\Lambda(f)+\epsilon)^n$; see \cite[Lemma~5 and End of the proof of Theorem~1]{DS05a}.
We refer to \cref{cor:volume-growth} for a slightly stronger bound with $d$ replaced by the length of the interval of maximal dynamical degrees.
          
                                                                                                                                                                  
Furthermore, in \cite{HS-ht-growth}, we apply the present method to establish a similar height growth of rational self-maps over number fields via Yuan--Zhang's arithmetic intersection theory \cite{YZ26}.

label: thm:strict-break-asymptotics
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: rmk:strict-break-sharpness
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:strict-break-sharpness}
Because \eqref{eq:main-asymptotic} holds for every $\eta>s_i(f)$, it is equivalent to
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left|\deg_{i,\omega}(f^n)-C_{f,\omega,i}\,\lambda_i(f)^n\right|^{1/n}\leq s_i(f).
\]
The threshold $s_i(f)$ in the above estimate is optimal.
However, one cannot replace the remainder in \eqref{eq:main-asymptotic} by $O\bigl(s_i(f)^n\bigr)$ in general.
For every $d\geq3$ and every $1\leq i\leq d-1$, we construct an isogeny of a power of an elliptic curve for which the remainder is asymptotic to a nonzero multiple of $ns_i(f)^n$; see \cref{prop:abelian-endpoint-failure}.
head: environment

label: rmk:strict-break-consequences
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:strict-break-consequences}
\Cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics} also yields exponential convergence of successive degree ratios $\deg_{i,\omega}(f^{n+1})/\deg_{i,\omega}(f^n)$; see \cref{cor:quotient}.
It further gives a meromorphic continuation of the $i$-th degree generating series 
\[
\mathcal{D}_{i,f,\omega}(z)\coloneqq \sum_{n\geq0}\deg_{i,\omega}(f^n)z^n
\]
to the disk $|z|<s_i(f)^{-1}$, with a unique simple pole at $z=\lambda_i(f)^{-1}$; see \cref{cor:generating-series}.
In the projective setting, the continuation radius $s_i(f)^{-1}$ is optimal in every dimension and intermediate codimension when $\operatorname{char}(\mathbf{k})\neq2$; see \cref{rmk:BDJ-Nguyen}.

label: thm:degree-log-laplacian
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: rmk:proof-outline
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:proof-outline}
We briefly outline the proofs.
For each finite orbit segment, we work over a normalized projective orbit variety or a compact K\"ahler resolution of the corresponding analytic orbit space.
These spaces are variants of the iterated graphs used in \cite{Gromov03,Friedland91,DS05a,DS08}.
The coordinate pullbacks of $\omega$ are nef and big, adjacent coordinate classes are uniformly comparable in the pseudo-effective order, and a two-time shift identity converts mixed intersections at times $m$ and $\ell$ into degrees of $f^{\ell-m}$ multiplied by $\lambda_d(f)^m$.
Together, these data form an ordered Hodge--Lorentz package in the sense of \cref{def:ordered-HL}.

The four-point Ptolemy inequality controls the determinant appearing in a mixed logarithmic derivative of the moving intersection function.
Integrating over the parameter square then yields the uniform estimate \eqref{eq:degree-log-laplacian}.
At a strict dynamical-degree break, the $n$-th root of the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:degree-log-laplacian} tends to $s_i(f)/\lambda_i(f)<1$.
The logarithmic slopes of the degree sequence are therefore exponentially Cauchy, and an elementary lemma on sequences proves \cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics}.

On a maximal affine interval $[r,s]$, the normalized degree sequences at its endpoints are bounded by \cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics}.
Combining the same temporal estimate \eqref{eq:degree-log-laplacian} with a discrete Phragm\'en--Lindel\"of argument \cref{lemma:two-variable-maximum-principle} gives the polynomial upper bound with exponent $2(i-r)(s-i)$ for the normalized degree sequences.
This can be regarded as a two-variable maximum principle.

label: def:ordered-HL
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:ordered-HL}
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space, let $\mathcal{N}\subseteq\mathcal{P}\subseteq V$ be nonempty convex cones containing the origin, and let $Q\colon V^d\to\mathbf{R}$ be a symmetric multilinear form, where $d\geq2$.
We call $(V,\mathcal{N},\mathcal{P},Q)$ an \emph{ordered Hodge--Lorentz package} of degree $d$ if the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item \label{def:ordered-HL-i} Nonnegativity: For every $\xi\in\mathcal{P}$ and $\eta_2,\ldots,\eta_d\in\mathcal{N}$,
\[
Q(\xi,\eta_2,\ldots,\eta_d)\geq0.
\]
\item \label{def:ordered-HL-ii} Lorentzian: For every $\eta_3,\ldots,\eta_d\in\mathcal{N}$, the symmetric bilinear form
\[
\mathscr{B}\colon V\times V \to \mathbf{R}, \quad (v_1,v_2)\longmapsto Q(v_1,v_2,\eta_3,\ldots,\eta_d)
\]
has positive index at most one.
\end{enumerate}
We write $v_1\preceq_{\mathcal{P}}v_2$ if $v_2-v_1\in\mathcal{P}$; this is the preorder induced by $\mathcal{P}$.
head: environment

label: prop:geometric-HL
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:geometric-HL}
The following are ordered Hodge--Lorentz packages.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\alph*)}]
\item If $Y$ is a normal projective variety of dimension $d\ge2$ over an algebraically closed field, take
\[
V=\mathsf{N}^1(Y)_\mathbf{R},\qquad
\mathcal{N}=\operatorname{Nef}^1(Y),\qquad
\mathcal{P}=\operatorname{Psef}^1(Y),
\]
and
\[
Q(D_1,\ldots,D_d)=(D_1\cdots D_d)_Y.
\]
\item If $Y$ is a compact K\"ahler manifold of dimension $d\ge2$, take
\[
V=H^{1,1}(Y,\mathbf{R}),\qquad
\mathcal{N}=\overline{\mathcal{K}}(Y),\qquad
\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{E}(Y),
\]
and
\[
Q(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_d)=\int_Y\alpha_1\wedge\cdots\wedge\alpha_d.
\]
\end{enumerate}
In either realization, the mixed intersection of nef and big classes is strictly positive.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the projective case, an effective $\mathbf{R}$-Cartier divisor has nonnegative intersection with ample divisors.
Approximating the nef divisor classes $\eta_2,\ldots,\eta_d$ by ample classes and the pseudo-effective divisor class $\xi$ by effective classes shows that a pseudo-effective divisor has nonnegative intersection with nef divisors.
For frozen ample classes $h_3,\ldots,h_d$, the arbitrary-characteristic mixed Hodge index theorem (see \cite[Proposition~2.9]{Hu20a}; cf. \cite[Variant~1.6.2 and Remark~1.6.5]{Lazarsfeld-I}, \cite[Theorem~5.20]{YZ17}) shows that the resulting bilinear form $\mathscr{B}$ is negative definite on the primitive hyperplane
\[
\{v\in V:Q(v,h,h_3,\ldots,h_d)=0\}
\]
for any ample class $h$, while $Q(h,h,h_3,\ldots,h_d)>0$.
The form therefore has positive index one.
Replacing frozen nef divisor classes $\eta_j$, with $3\le j\le d$, by $\eta_j+\epsilon h$ and letting $\epsilon\to 0^+$ proves that the positive index is at most one in the nef case.

In the compact K\"ahler case, represent a pseudo-effective class by a positive closed $(1,1)$-current and first pair it with K\"ahler forms.
Approximating each nef class by K\"ahler classes and passing to the limit verifies the nonnegativity condition~\ref{def:ordered-HL-i}.
For frozen K\"ahler classes, the mixed Hodge--Riemann theorem \cite{Gromov90,DN06} yields negative definiteness on the corresponding primitive hyperplane, and hence the positive index one assertion.
          
Approximating the frozen nef classes $\eta_3,\ldots,\eta_d$ by K\"ahler classes again proves that the positive index is at most one.

It remains to show strict positivity.
Fix an ample class in the projective case and a K\"ahler class in the analytic case, and denote it by $h$.
If $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d$ are nef and big, then for suitable $\epsilon_j>0$ the classes $\omega_j-\epsilon_jh$ are pseudo-effective.
Repeatedly applying the nonnegativity condition~\ref{def:ordered-HL-i} yields
\[
Q(\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_d)\geq\epsilon_1\cdots\epsilon_d\,Q(h,\ldots,h)>0.
\qedhere
\]

label: lemma:Ptolemy
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $b_{ij}=\mathscr{B}(v_i,v_j)$ and let $G=(b_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq4}$ be the Gram matrix.
                                                                                                                    
Its positive index is at most that of $\mathscr{B}$, hence at most one.
The matrix
\[
M=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&b_{12}&b_{13}&b_{14}\\
b_{12}&0&b_{23}&b_{24}\\
b_{13}&b_{23}&0&b_{34}\\
b_{14}&b_{24}&b_{34}&0
\end{pmatrix}
\]
satisfies $M=G-\mathrm{diag}(b_{11},\ldots,b_{44})$.
                                                                                               
Since $b_{ii}\ge0$ for all $1\le i\le 4$, $M$ has positive index at most one.
If $M$ is nonsingular, its zero trace forces its signature to be $(1,3)$, and hence $\det M<0$; if it is singular, $\det M=0$.
Thus $\det M\leq0$.
Set
\[
a=\sqrt{b_{12}b_{34}},\qquad
b=\sqrt{b_{13}b_{24}},\qquad
c=\sqrt{b_{14}b_{23}}.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
\det M=\bigl(b^2-(a+c)^2\bigr)\bigl(b^2-(a-c)^2\bigr).
\]
Since $(a-c)^2\leq(a+c)^2$, the inequality $\det M\leq0$ is equivalent to
\[
(a-c)^2\leq b^2 \leq (a+c)^2.
\]
Thus $|a-c|\leq b \le a+c$.
The first inequality is exactly \eqref{eq:four-point-Ptolemy}.

label: prop:Ptolemy-estimate-unit-square
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: eq:comparison-AsA0A1-BtB0B1
title: Proof
body_md:
By the comparison hypotheses \eqref{eq:comparison-A0A1-B0B1} and convexity of $\mathcal{P}$, we have for $s,t\in[0,1]$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:comparison-AsA0A1-BtB0B1}
A_0,A_1\preceq_{\mathcal{P}}KA_s,\qquad
B_0,B_1\preceq_{\mathcal{P}}KB_t.
\end{equation}
Indeed,
\[
KA_s-A_0=(K-1)(1-s)A_0+s(KA_1-A_0)\in\mathcal{P},
\]
and the other three comparisons are identical.

Note that $\Phi_i$ is a polynomial in $s$ and $t$.
Hence positivity of $\Phi_i$ on $[0,1]^2$ implies that $\log\Phi_i$ is smooth on an open neighborhood of $[0,1]^2$.
Fix $(s,t)\in[0,1]^2$ so that $A_s,B_t\in\mathcal{N}$.
Define a symmetric bilinear form on $V$ by
\[
\mathscr{B}(v_1,v_2)\coloneqq Q\bigl(v_1,v_2,A_s^{[d-i-1]},B_t^{[i-1]}\bigr).
\]
The form $\mathscr{B}$ has positive index at most one by \cref{def:ordered-HL}\ref{def:ordered-HL-ii}, and $\Phi_i(s,t)=\mathscr{B}(A_s,B_t)$.
By multilinearity and taking partial derivatives of $\Phi_i$, we have
\[
\partial_s\Phi_i=(d-i)\mathscr{B}(u,B_t),\qquad
\partial_t\Phi_i=i\mathscr{B}(A_s,v),\qquad
\partial_s\partial_t\Phi_i=i(d-i)\mathscr{B}(u,v),
\]
where $u\coloneqq A_1-A_0$ and $v\coloneqq B_1-B_0$.
It follows that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-hessian}
\partial_s\partial_t\log\Phi_i(s,t)
=i(d-i)\frac{\mathscr{B}(A_s,B_t)\mathscr{B}(u,v)-\mathscr{B}(A_s,v)\mathscr{B}(u,B_t)}{\mathscr{B}(A_s,B_t)^2}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, bilinearity of $\mathscr{B}$ yields the following matrix identity:
\[
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathscr{B}(A_s,B_t)&\mathscr{B}(A_s,v)\\
\mathscr{B}(u,B_t)&\mathscr{B}(u,v)
\end{pmatrix}
=\begin{pmatrix}
1-s&s\\
-1&1
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_0)&\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_1)\\
\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_0)&\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_1)
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1-t&-1\\
t&1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Taking determinants and substituting back to \eqref{eq:log-hessian}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:log-hessian-2}
\partial_s\partial_t\log\Phi_i(s,t)=
i(d-i)\frac{\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_0)\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_1)-\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_1)\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_0)}{\mathscr{B}(A_s,B_t)^2}.
\end{equation}

All pairings among $A_0,B_0,A_1,B_1$ under $\mathscr{B}$ are nonnegative by \cref{def:ordered-HL}\ref{def:ordered-HL-i}.
Applying the four-point Ptolemy inequality, \cref{lemma:Ptolemy}, to $A_0,B_0,A_1,B_1$, and then multiplying by the sum of the two square roots in the left-hand side, we get
\begin{align}\label{eq:Ptolemy-A01B01}
\begin{split}
&\qquad\qquad\bigl|
\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_0)\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_1)-\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_1)\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_0)\bigr|\\
&\leq\sqrt{\mathscr{B}(A_0,A_1)\mathscr{B}(B_0,B_1)}\,\Bigl(\sqrt{\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_0)\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_1)}+\sqrt{\mathscr{B}(A_0,B_1)\mathscr{B}(A_1,B_0)}\Bigr).
\end{split}
\end{align}
Use the comparison \eqref{eq:comparison-AsA0A1-BtB0B1} to bound the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:Ptolemy-A01B01} as follows:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:AsBt-comparison}
\begin{aligned}
\mathscr{B}(A_0,A_1) &\le K \mathscr{B}(A_s,A_1) \le K^2 \mathscr{B}(A_s,A_s) = K^2 \Phi_{i-1}(s,t),\\[2pt]
\mathscr{B}(B_0,B_1) &\le K \mathscr{B}(B_t,B_1) \le K^2 \mathscr{B}(B_t,B_t) = K^2 \Phi_{i+1}(s,t),\\[2pt]
\mathscr{B}(A_j,B_k) &\le K^2 \mathscr{B}(A_s,B_t) = K^2 \Phi_i(s,t),\qquad
j,k\in \{0,1\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Substituting the estimates \eqref{eq:Ptolemy-A01B01} and \eqref{eq:AsBt-comparison} into \eqref{eq:log-hessian-2}, we prove \eqref{eq:uniform-Ptolemy-unit-square}.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The estimate only requires the four classes to belong to the formal nef cone $\mathcal{N}$.
In dynamical applications, these classes are also big so that mutual comparison \eqref{eq:comparison-A0A1-B0B1} in the pseudo-effective order and positivity of $\Phi_i$ on $[0,1]^2$ hold simultaneously.

label: thm:abstract-log-laplacian
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:abstract-log-laplacian}
Fix integers $d,N\geq2$.
Let $(V,\mathcal{N},\mathcal{P},Q)$ be an ordered Hodge--Lorentz package of degree $d\geq2$, and let $\eta_0,\ldots,\eta_N\in\mathcal{N}$.
Suppose that there exist constants $K\geq1$ and $\lambda_d>0$, and positive numbers
\[
\delta_j(m)>0,\qquad
0\leq j\leq d,\ 0\leq m\leq N,
\]
such that the following hypotheses hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item\label{thm:abstract-log-laplacian-comparison}
For every $0\leq m<N$,
\[
K^{-1}\eta_m\preceq_{\mathcal{P}}\eta_{m+1}\preceq_{\mathcal{P}} K\eta_m.
\]

\item\label{thm:abstract-log-laplacian-two-time-shift}
For every $0\leq m\leq\ell\leq N$ and $0\leq j\leq d$,
\[
Q\bigl(\eta_m^{[d-j]},\eta_\ell^{[j]}\bigr)=\lambda_d^m\delta_j(\ell-m).
\]
\end{enumerate}
Then for every $1\leq i\leq d-1$ and $1\leq n\leq N-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-log-laplacian}
\left|\log\frac{\delta_i(n)^2}{\delta_i(n-1)\delta_i(n+1)}\right|
\leq 2i(d-i)K^{2d+4}\frac{\sqrt{\delta_{i-1}(n)\delta_{i+1}(n)}}{\delta_i(n)}.
\end{equation}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $1\leq i\leq d-1$ and $1\leq n\leq N-1$.
We apply \cref{prop:Ptolemy-estimate-unit-square} to
\[
\eta_0,\eta_1,\eta_n,\eta_{n+1}\in\mathcal{N}.
\]
For $s,t\in[0,1]$, set
\[
\eta_s\coloneqq(1-s)\eta_0+s\eta_1,\qquad
\eta_{n+t}\coloneqq(1-t)\eta_n+t\eta_{n+1},
\]
and for $0\leq j\leq d$,
\[
\Phi_j(s,t)\coloneqq Q\bigl(\eta_s^{[d-j]},\eta_{n+t}^{[j]}\bigr).
\]

The hypothesis~\ref{thm:abstract-log-laplacian-comparison}, applied at $m=0$ and $m=n$, verifies \eqref{eq:comparison-A0A1-B0B1} and implies
\[
K^{-1}\eta_0\preceq_{\mathcal{P}} \eta_s \preceq_{\mathcal{P}} K\eta_0,\qquad
K^{-1}\eta_n \preceq_{\mathcal{P}} \eta_{n+t} \preceq_{\mathcal{P}} K\eta_n.
\]
By multilinearity, the nonnegativity condition in \cref{def:ordered-HL}\ref{def:ordered-HL-i}, and the hypothesis~\ref{thm:abstract-log-laplacian-two-time-shift} here, we have for every $0\leq j\leq d$ and $(s,t)\in[0,1]^2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-moving-degree-comparison}
K^{-d}\delta_j(n)\leq \Phi_j(s,t)\leq K^d\delta_j(n).
\end{equation}
In particular, $\Phi_i$ is positive on $[0,1]^2$.

Applying \cref{prop:Ptolemy-estimate-unit-square} and then using \eqref{eq:abstract-moving-degree-comparison}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-uniform-unit-square}
\begin{aligned}
\bigl|\partial_s\partial_t\log\Phi_i(s,t)\bigr|
&\leq 2i(d-i)K^4 \frac{\sqrt{\Phi_{i-1}(s,t)\Phi_{i+1}(s,t)}}{\Phi_i(s,t)}\\
&\leq 2i(d-i)K^{2d+4} \frac{\sqrt{\delta_{i-1}(n)\delta_{i+1}(n)}}{\delta_i(n)}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By hypothesis~\ref{thm:abstract-log-laplacian-two-time-shift}, the four corner values are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_i(0,0)&=\delta_i(n), &\quad\Phi_i(1,0)&=\lambda_d\delta_i(n-1),\\
\Phi_i(0,1)&=\delta_i(n+1), & \quad\Phi_i(1,1)&=\lambda_d\delta_i(n).
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence the fundamental theorem of calculus yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1\!\int_0^1\partial_s\partial_t\log\Phi_i(s,t)\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} s\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} t
&=\log\frac{\Phi_i(1,1)\Phi_i(0,0)}{\Phi_i(1,0)\Phi_i(0,1)}\\
&=\log\frac{\delta_i(n)^2}{\delta_i(n-1)\delta_i(n+1)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
By integrating \eqref{eq:abstract-uniform-unit-square} and the triangle inequality, we prove \eqref{eq:abstract-log-laplacian}.

label: lemma:projective-pullback-positivity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:projective-pullback-positivity}
Let $\varphi\colon Y\to Z$ be a surjective morphism of normal projective varieties.
Then pullback preserves pseudo-effective and nef divisor classes.
If, moreover, $\varphi$ is generically finite, then it also preserves nef and big divisor classes.

label: lemma:projective-two-time-shift
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:projective-two-time-shift-diagram
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $0\leq i\leq d$ and $0\leq m\leq\ell\leq N$.
Set $k=\ell-m$.
If $m=\ell$, then the projection formula yields
\[
\bigl(\omega_{m,N}^d\bigr)_{Y_N}=\deg(\pi_{m,N})(\omega^d)_X=\lambda_d(f)^m\deg_i(f^0),
\]
so \eqref{eq:projective-two-time-shift} holds.
We thus assume that $m<\ell$.
The image of the two-coordinate morphism
\[
(\pi_{m,N},\pi_{\ell,N})\colon Y_N\longrightarrow X\times X
\]
is the graph closure $\Gamma_k$ of $f^k$.
Indeed, over a dense open subset $U_N \subseteq X$, its image consists of
\[
\bigl(f^m(x),f^\ell(x)\bigr)=\bigl(x_m,f^k(x_m)\bigr),\qquad
x_m\coloneqq f^m(x).
\]
Since $f^m$ is dominant, these points are dense in $\Gamma_k$.
We thus think of $(\pi_{m,N},\pi_{\ell,N})$ as a surjective generically finite morphism from $Y_N$ to $\Gamma_k$.
Because $Y_N$ is normal, by the universal property of normalization, the morphism $(\pi_{m,N},\pi_{\ell,N})$ factors uniquely through the normalization $\widetilde\Gamma_k$ as a surjective generically finite morphism
\[
\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\colon Y_N\longrightarrow\widetilde\Gamma_k
\]
with
\[
\pi_{m,N}=p_k\circ\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)},\qquad
\pi_{\ell,N}=q_k\circ\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}.
\]
In other words, we have the following commutative diagram
\begin{equation}\label{eq:projective-two-time-shift-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=5.2em, row sep=4.2em]
& Y_N \arrow[dl, swap, "\pi_{m,N}"] \arrow[d, "\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}"'] \arrow[dr, "\pi_{\ell,N}"] & \\
X & \widetilde\Gamma_k \arrow[l, "p_k"'] \arrow[r, "q_k"] & X.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

Because $p_k$ is birational, $\deg\bigl(\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\bigr)=\deg(\pi_{m,N})=\lambda_d(f)^m$.
The projection formula therefore yields
\begin{align*}
\bigl(\omega_{m,N}^{d-i}\cdot \omega_{\ell,N}^i\bigr)_{Y_N}=
\deg\bigl(\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\bigr)\bigl((p_k^*\omega)^{d-i}\cdot(q_k^*\omega)^i\bigr)_{\widetilde\Gamma_k}
=\lambda_d(f)^m\deg_i(f^k),
\end{align*}
which proves \eqref{eq:projective-two-time-shift}.

\[

label: lemma:kahler-pullback-positivity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:kahler-pullback-positivity}
Let $\varphi\colon Y\to Z$ be a surjective holomorphic map between compact K\"ahler manifolds.
Then pullback preserves the pseudo-effective cone and the nef cone:
\[
\varphi^*\mathcal{E}(Z)\subseteq\mathcal{E}(Y),\qquad
\varphi^*\overline{\mathcal{K}}(Z)\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{K}}(Y).
\]
If, moreover, $\varphi$ is generically finite, then the pullback of every nef and big class on $Z$ is nef and big on $Y$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion follows from \cite[Proposition~III.1.19 and Theorem~I.5.11]{Demailly-agbook}.
Indeed, let $\alpha\in\mathcal{E}(Z)$, and choose a positive closed $(1,1)$-current $T$ representing $\alpha$, locally, of the form
\[
T=\mathrm{d}\mathrm{d}^c u,
\]
where $u$ is plurisubharmonic.
Since $\varphi$ is surjective, $u\circ\varphi$ is not identically $-\infty$, and the pullback current $\varphi^*T$ is locally of the form $\mathrm{d}\mathrm{d}^c(u\circ\varphi)$, which is a positive closed $(1,1)$-current representing $\varphi^*\alpha$.
Thus $\varphi^*\alpha$ is pseudo-effective.

Now let $\alpha\in\overline{\mathcal{K}}(Z)$ be nef.
Fix K\"ahler forms $\omega_Y$ and $\omega_Z$ on $Y$ and $Z$, respectively.
For every $\epsilon>0$, there is a smooth representative $\alpha_\epsilon$ of $\alpha$ such that
\[
\alpha_\epsilon\geq-\epsilon\omega_Z.
\]
Since $Y$ is compact and $\omega_Y$ is a K\"ahler form, the form $\varphi^*\omega_Z$ is bounded above by $C\omega_Y$ for some $C>0$.
It follows that
\[
\varphi^*\alpha_\epsilon\geq -\epsilon\varphi^*\omega_Z\geq -C\epsilon\omega_Y,
\]
so $\varphi^*\alpha\in\overline{\mathcal{K}}(Y)$ is nef.

Finally, suppose further that $\varphi$ is generically finite and that $\alpha$ is nef and big.
Set $d=\dim Y=\dim Z$.
Then the projection formula yields
\[
\int_Y(\varphi^*\alpha)^d
=
\deg(\varphi)\int_Z\alpha^d
>0.
\]
Since $\varphi^*\alpha$ is nef, it is big by \cite[Theorem~0.5]{DP04}.

label: eq:kahler-pi-varphi
title: Proof
body_md:
If $m=\ell$, then by the projection formula and \eqref{eq:kahler-coordinate-degree},
\[
\int_{Y_N}\omega_{m,N}^d=\deg(\pi_{m,N})\int_X\omega^d=\lambda_d(f)^m\deg_i(f^0),
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:kahler-two-time-shift}.
We thus assume that $m<\ell$.
Set $k\coloneqq\ell-m$.
Similarly, the two-coordinate map
\[
\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\coloneqq(\pi_{m,N},\pi_{\ell,N})\colon Y_N\longrightarrow X\times X
\]
has image equal to $\Gamma_k$.
Indeed, on the dense regular-orbit locus,
\[
\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}(x)=\bigl(f^m(x),f^\ell(x)\bigr)=\bigl(x_m,f^k(x_m)\bigr),\qquad
x_m\coloneqq f^m(x),
\]
and these points are dense in $\Gamma_k$ because $f^m$ is dominant.
We therefore regard $\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}$ as a surjective holomorphic map
\[
\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\colon Y_N\longrightarrow\Gamma_k.
\]
Moreover, by the definition of $\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kahler-pi-varphi}
\pi_{m,N}=(\operatorname{pr}_0|_{\Gamma_k})\circ\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)},\qquad
\pi_{\ell,N}=(\operatorname{pr}_1|_{\Gamma_k})\circ\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}.
\end{equation}

Since $\operatorname{pr}_0|_{\Gamma_k} \colon \Gamma_k \to X$ is bimeromorphic, we have
\[
\deg\bigl(\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\bigr)=\deg(\pi_{m,N})=\lambda_d(f)^m,
\]
where the last equality is \eqref{eq:kahler-coordinate-degree}.
It follows that
\[
\bigl(\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\bigr)_*[Y_N]=\lambda_d(f)^m[\Gamma_k].
\]
Therefore, by the projection formula and \eqref{eq:kahler-degree-current}, we obtain
\begin{align*}
\int_{Y_N}\omega_{m,N}^{d-i}\wedge\omega_{\ell,N}^i
&= \Bigl\langle\bigl(\varphi_{m,\ell}^{(N)}\bigr)_*[Y_N], \, \operatorname{pr}_0^*\omega^{d-i}\wedge\operatorname{pr}_1^*\omega^i \Bigr\rangle\\
&= \lambda_d(f)^m \Bigl\langle [\Gamma_k], \, \operatorname{pr}_0^*\omega^{d-i}\wedge\operatorname{pr}_1^*\omega^i \Bigr\rangle\\
&= \lambda_d(f)^m\deg_i(f^k).\qedhere
\end{align*}

label: lemma:kahler-adjacent-comparison
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:kahler-fixed-graph-comparison
title: Proof
body_md:
The classes $p_1^*\omega$ and $q_1^*\omega$ are nef and big on the fixed compact K\"ahler manifold $\widetilde\Gamma_1$.
Since the big cone is the interior of the pseudo-effective cone, there is a constant $K_{f,\omega}\geq1$, depending only on $p_1^*\omega$ and $q_1^*\omega$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kahler-fixed-graph-comparison}
K_{f,\omega}^{-1}\,p_1^*\omega\preceq_{\widetilde\Gamma_1}q_1^*\omega\preceq_{\widetilde\Gamma_1}K_{f,\omega}\,p_1^*\omega.
\end{equation}

Fix $N\geq1$ and $0\leq m<N$.
The adjacent-coordinate map
\[
\varphi_{m,m+1}^{(N)}\coloneqq(\pi_{m,N},\pi_{m+1,N})\colon Y_N\longrightarrow X\times X
\]
has image equal to $\Gamma_1$, and we regard it as a surjective holomorphic map $Y_N\to\Gamma_1$.

Recall that $\sigma_1\colon\widetilde\Gamma_1\to\Gamma_1$ is bimeromorphic, so that we have a meromorphic lift
\[
\sigma_1^{-1}\circ\varphi_{m,m+1}^{(N)}\colon Y_N\dashrightarrow \widetilde{\Gamma}_1.
\]
After resolving its indeterminacy, we obtain a compact K\"ahler manifold $W_{m,N}$, a bimeromorphic morphism $\tau_{m,N}\colon W_{m,N}\to Y_N$, and a surjective holomorphic map $\psi_{m,N}\colon W_{m,N}\to\widetilde\Gamma_1$, such that the following diagram commutes:
\[
\begin{tikzcd}
W_{m,N} \arrow[r, "\psi_{m,N}"] \arrow[d, "\tau_{m,N}"'] & \widetilde{\Gamma}_1 \arrow[d, "\sigma_1"]\\
Y_N \arrow[r, "\varphi_{m,m+1}^{(N)}"'] & \Gamma_1.
\end{tikzcd}
\]
Moreover, by \eqref{eq:kahler-pnqn} and \eqref{eq:kahler-pi-varphi}, we have
\begin{align*}
p_1\circ\psi_{m,N}&=(\operatorname{pr}_0|_{\Gamma_1})\circ\sigma_1\circ\psi_{m,N}=(\operatorname{pr}_0|_{\Gamma_1})\circ\varphi_{m,m+1}^{(N)}\circ\tau_{m,N}=\pi_{m,N}\circ\tau_{m,N},\\
q_1\circ\psi_{m,N}&=(\operatorname{pr}_1|_{\Gamma_1})\circ\sigma_1\circ\psi_{m,N}=(\operatorname{pr}_1|_{\Gamma_1})\circ\varphi_{m,m+1}^{(N)}\circ\tau_{m,N}=\pi_{m+1,N}\circ\tau_{m,N}.
\end{align*}
It follows that
\[
\tau_{m,N}^*\omega_{m,N}=\psi_{m,N}^*p_1^*\omega,\qquad
\tau_{m,N}^*\omega_{m+1,N}=\psi_{m,N}^*q_1^*\omega.
\]
Thus pulling back the comparison \eqref{eq:kahler-fixed-graph-comparison} by $\psi_{m,N}$ and applying \cref{lemma:kahler-pullback-positivity} yield
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kahler-comparison-on-WmN}
K_{f,\omega}^{-1}\,\tau_{m,N}^*\omega_{m,N}\preceq_{W_{m,N}}\tau_{m,N}^*\omega_{m+1,N}\preceq_{W_{m,N}}K_{f,\omega}\,\tau_{m,N}^*\omega_{m,N}.
\end{equation}
Since $\tau_{m,N}$ is bimeromorphic and holomorphic, $(\tau_{m,N})_*\tau_{m,N}^*=\operatorname{id}$ on $H^{1,1}(Y_N,\mathbf{R})$.
By taking pushforward $(\tau_{m,N})_*$ in \eqref{eq:kahler-comparison-on-WmN}, we prove \eqref{eq:kahler-adjacent-comparison}.

label: lemma:discrete-integration
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma:discrete-integration}
Let $(a_n)_{n\geq0}$ be a sequence of positive real numbers such that
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty}a_n^{1/n}=\alpha>0.
\]
Suppose that for some $0<q<1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-kappa-bound}
\left|\log\frac{a_n^2}{a_{n-1}a_{n+1}}\right|=O(q^n).
\end{equation}
Then
\[
a_n=C\alpha^n\bigl(1+O(q^n)\bigr),
\]
where
\[
C=a_0\exp\!\left(\sum_{m\geq1}m \log\frac{a_m^2}{a_{m-1}a_{m+1}}\right)
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n}{\alpha^n}
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{a_n^{n+1}}{a_{n+1}^n},
\]
and the series converges absolutely.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Denote for all appropriate $n$,
\[
b_n\coloneqq\log a_n,\qquad
c_n\coloneqq b_n-b_{n-1}=\log\frac{a_n}{a_{n-1}},\qquad
\kappa_n\coloneqq c_n-c_{n+1}=\log\frac{a_n^2}{a_{n-1}a_{n+1}}.
\]
Then the assumed \eqref{eq:abstract-kappa-bound} says that $|\kappa_n|=O(q^n)$.
Hence $(c_n)_{n\geq1}$ is an exponentially Cauchy sequence and converges to some $c\in\mathbf{R}$, with
\[
c_n-c=\sum_{m\geq n}\kappa_m=O(q^n).
\]
By the Stolz--Ces\`aro theorem and the root-limit assumption, we have
\[
c=\lim_{n\to\infty}c_n
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{b_n}{n}
=\lim_{n\to\infty}\log(a_n^{1/n})
=\log\alpha.
\]
Moreover, since $\sum_{m\geq1}m\kappa_m$ converges absolutely,
\[
\sum_{n\geq1}(c_n-\log\alpha)=\sum_{n\geq1}\sum_{m\geq n}\kappa_m=\sum_{m\geq1}m\kappa_m.
\]
Define
\[
C\coloneqq a_0\exp\!\left(\sum_{m\geq1}m\kappa_m\right)\in\mathbf{R}_{>0}.
\]
We thus obtain
\[
\log\frac{a_n}{C\alpha^n}=b_n-b_0-n\log\alpha-\sum_{m\geq1}m\kappa_m=-\sum_{m>n}(c_m-\log\alpha)=O(q^n).
\]
Taking exponentiation, we get
\[
a_n=C\alpha^n\exp\bigl(O(q^n)\bigr)=C\alpha^n\bigl(1+O(q^n)\bigr).
\]
This asymptotic also yields $a_n/\alpha^n\to C$.
Finally, direct telescoping gives, for $n\geq1$,
\[
a_0\exp\!\left(\sum_{m=1}^nm\kappa_m\right)=\frac{a_n^{n+1}}{a_{n+1}^n}.
\]
By letting $n\to\infty$, we prove the remaining formula for $C$.

Recall that in either setting, the limits defining dynamical degrees exist, i.e., for every $0\leq j\leq d$,

label: eq:C2
title: Proof
body_md:
If $s-r=1$, then the conclusion follows immediately from \eqref{eq:affine-interval-bounded} with $C'_{u,r,s}=C_1$.
We therefore assume that $s-r\geq2$.

Denote $b_i\coloneqq 2(i-r)(s-i)$ and choose $C_2,C_3\ge1$ such that
\begin{align}
C_2 &\geq \max\Bigl\{C_1, \, \max_{r\le i\le s}\{u_{i,1}\}\Bigr\} \label{eq:C2}, \\
C_0C_3^{-2}&<\min_{r<j<s}b_j=2(s-r-1). \label{eq:C3}
\end{align}
We shall show that it suffices to take $\displaystyle C'_{u,r,s}\geq C_2 + \frac{1}{2}(s-r)^2\log C_3$.
                   
   
                                                                                                                                  
   

For $r\le i\le s$ and $n\geq1$, define
\[
v_{i,n}\coloneqq C_2+b_i\log(C_3n).
\]
By \eqref{eq:affine-interval-bounded} and the choice \eqref{eq:C2} of $C_2$, $u\le v$ on the boundary of the discrete half-strip $\{r,\ldots,s\}\times\mathbf{Z}_{n\geq1}$, i.e., $u_{i,n}\le v_{i,n}$ for $i=r,s$, or $n=1$.

Fix an arbitrary auxiliary $\epsilon>0$.
For $r\le i\le s$ and $n\geq1$, set
\[
w_{i,n}\coloneqq u_{i,n}-v_{i,n}-\epsilon n.
\]
Then according to \eqref{eq:affine-interval-root-limit}, $\displaystyle\lim_{n\to\infty}w_{i,n}=-\infty$ uniformly for all $r\le i\le s$.
If $w$ were positive somewhere, it would attain a positive global maximum at some $r<i_\circ<s$ and $n_\circ\geq2$.
It follows that $(\Delta_{\mathrm{sp}} w)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}\geq0$ and hence
\[
(\Delta_{\mathrm{sp}} u)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}\geq (\Delta_{\mathrm{sp}} v)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}=4\log(C_3n_\circ).
\]
Combining this with \eqref{eq:affine-interval-temporal-estimate} and \eqref{eq:C3} yields that
\[
\bigl|(\Delta_{\mathrm{tm}} u)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}\bigr|
\leq C_0\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2}(\Delta_{\mathrm{sp}} u)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}\Bigr)
\leq \frac{C_0 C_3^{-2}}{n_\circ^2}
<\frac{b_{i_\circ}}{n_\circ^2}.
\]
On the other hand, by $(\Delta_{\mathrm{tm}} w)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}\geq0$ and the fact that $\log(1+x)\le x$ for $x>-1$, one has
\[
(\Delta_{\mathrm{tm}} u)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}\geq(\Delta_{\mathrm{tm}} v)_{i_\circ,n_\circ}=b_{i_\circ}\log\frac{n_\circ^2}{n_\circ^2-1}=-b_{i_\circ}\log\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{n_\circ^2}\Bigr)\geq\frac{b_{i_\circ}}{n_\circ^2},
\]
a contradiction.
It follows that $w\leq0$, i.e., for every $r\le i\le s$ and $n\geq1$,
\[
u_{i,n}\leq v_{i,n}+\epsilon n.
\]
Since both $u$ and $v$ are independent of $\epsilon$, by letting $\epsilon\to0^+$, we obtain
\[
u_{i,n}\leq v_{i,n}=C_2+b_i\log C_3+b_i\log n\leq C'_{u,r,s}+b_i\log n.\qedhere
\]

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix a maximal affine interval $[r,s]$ of $(\log\lambda_i(f))_i$, and set
\[
u_{i,n}\coloneqq\log\frac{\deg_i(f^n)}{\lambda_i(f)^n},\qquad
r\leq i\leq s,\quad n\geq0.
\]
By the definition \eqref{eq:intro-dynamical-degree} of the dynamical degrees $\lambda_i(f)$, for every $r\le i\le s$,
\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{u_{i,n}}{n}=0.
\]

For every $r<j<s$, if any, the affineness of $[r,s]$ yields $\lambda_j(f)^2=\lambda_{j-1}(f)\lambda_{j+1}(f)$.
Hence by \cref{thm:degree-log-laplacian}, there is $C'_{f,\omega,j}>0$ such that for every $n\geq1$,
\[
\bigl|(\Delta_{\mathrm{tm}} u)_{j,n}\bigr|
\leq C'_{f,\omega,j}\, \frac{\sqrt{\deg_{j-1}(f^n)\deg_{j+1}(f^n)}}{\deg_j(f^n)}
=C'_{f,\omega,j}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{2}(\Delta_{\mathrm{sp}} u)_{j,n}\Bigr).
\]
Taking the maximum of the finitely many $C'_{f,\omega,j}$, we verify \eqref{eq:affine-interval-temporal-estimate} for $u$.

It remains to verify boundedness of $u$ at the boundary indices $i=r$ and $i=s$.
If $r>0$, then maximality of $[r,s]$, together with the log-concavity of the dynamical degrees, implies that $r$ is a strict dynamical-degree break, so \cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics} has shown that $(u_{r,n})_{n\geq0}$ is bounded (see also \cref{rmk:C-f-omega-i-limits}).
If $r=0$, then $u_{0,n}=\log\operatorname{vol}_X(\omega)$ is constant.
Similarly, $(u_{s,n})_n$ is bounded: if $s<d$, then $s$ is a strict break, while if $s=d$, then $u_{d,n}=\log\operatorname{vol}_X(\omega)$ is also constant.

Therefore, by \cref{lemma:two-variable-maximum-principle}, there is a constant $C'_{u,r,s}>0$ such that for every $r\leq i\leq s$ and $n\geq1$,
\[
u_{i,n}\leq C'_{u,r,s}+2(i-r)(s-i)\log n,
\]
or equivalently,
\[
\deg_i(f^n)\leq e^{C'_{u,r,s}}\, n^{2(i-r)(s-i)}\lambda_i(f)^n.
\]
Hence \eqref{eq:affine-interval-growth} holds with $C_{f,\omega,r,s}\coloneqq e^{C'_{u,r,s}}$.

Finally, note that every index $0\leq i\leq d$ lies in some maximal affine interval $[r,s]$ and $(i-r)(s-i)\leq i(d-i)$.
So by taking $C_{f,\omega}$ as the maximum of the finitely many $C_{f,\omega,r,s}$, the global estimate \eqref{eq:global-polynomial-growth} follows.
Combining \eqref{eq:global-polynomial-growth} with \eqref{eq:standard-exponential-lower-bound} and taking logarithms, we obtain \eqref{eq:global-log-growth}.
This concludes the proof of \cref{thm:affine-interval-growth}.

label: cor:volume-growth
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:volume-growth}
Assume that either \cref{setting:projective} or \cref{setting:kahler} holds.
Denote
                                                                  
\[
\Lambda(f)\coloneqq\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\lambda_i(f),\qquad I_{\max}\coloneqq\{i:\lambda_i(f)=\Lambda(f)\}=[r,s]\cap\mathbf{Z},\qquad \ell\coloneqq s-r.
\]
Then there are constants $c_{\operatorname{vol}},C_{\operatorname{vol}}>0$ such that for every $n\geq1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:volume-growth}
c_{\operatorname{vol}}\, \Lambda(f)^n\leq \operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})\leq C_{\operatorname{vol}}\, n^{(\ell^3+2\ell)/3}\Lambda(f)^n.
\end{equation}
In particular, if $f$ is cohomologically hyperbolic, then $\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})\asymp\Lambda(f)^n$; if $f$ has zero entropy, then $\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})=O\bigl(n^{(d^3+2d)/3}\bigr)$.

label: eq:volume-gap
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $n\geq 1$ and write $\omega_m\coloneqq\omega_{m,n}$ for $0\leq m\leq n$.
We first claim that for every ordered $d$-tuple $0\leq m_d\leq\dots\leq m_1\leq n$, one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:volume-gap}
\bigl(\omega_{m_1}\cdots\omega_{m_d}\bigr)_{Y_n}
\leq \frac{\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}2^{j(d-j)}}{(\omega^d)_X^{d}}\prod_{i=0}^{d}\deg_{i}(f^{k_i}),
\end{equation}
where $k_0=n-m_1$, $k_{j}=m_j-m_{j+1}$ for $1\leq j<d$, and $k_d=m_d$ (cf.~\cite[Equation~(3.3)]{CPR21}).
Indeed, for $1\leq j\leq d-1$, applying the reverse Khovanskii--Teissier inequality \cite[Theorem~2.5]{HX24} (cf.~\cite[Remark~3.1]{Xiao15}, \cite[Theorem~5.7]{LX17}, \cite[Theorem~3.4.3]{Dang20}, \cite[Theorem~3.5]{JL23})
                                                 
\[
\bigl(A^{d}\bigr)_{Y_n}\bigl(B_1\cdots B_d\bigr)_{Y_n}\le 2^{j(d-j)} \bigl(A^{d-j} B_1\cdots B_j\bigr)_{Y_n} \bigl(A^j B_{j+1}\cdots B_d\bigr)_{Y_n}
\]
with $A=\omega_{m_{j+1}}$, $B_1=\dots=B_j=\omega_{m_j}$, and $B_{j+1}=\omega_{m_{j+1}},\ldots,B_d=\omega_{m_d}$, we get
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Xiao-rKT}
\bigl(\omega_{m_{j+1}}^d\bigr)_{Y_n}\bigl(\omega_{m_j}^j\omega_{m_{j+1}}\cdots\omega_{m_d}\bigr)_{Y_n}
\leq 2^{j(d-j)}\bigl(\omega_{m_j}^j\omega_{m_{j+1}}^{d-j}\bigr)_{Y_n}\bigl(\omega_{m_{j+1}}^{j+1}\omega_{m_{j+2}}\cdots\omega_{m_d}\bigr)_{Y_n}.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, the two-time shift identity (see \cref{lemma:projective-two-time-shift,lemma:kahler-two-time-shift}) yields
\[
\bigl(\omega_{m_{j+1}}^d\bigr)_{Y_n}=(\omega^d)_X\lambda_d(f)^{m_{j+1}},\qquad \bigl(\omega_{m_j}^j\cdot\omega_{m_{j+1}}^{d-j}\bigr)_{Y_n}=\lambda_d(f)^{m_{j+1}}\deg_j(f^{k_j}).
\]
Iterating the preceding inequality \eqref{eq:Xiao-rKT} for $j=1,\ldots,d-1$ thus implies
\[
\bigl(\omega_{m_1}\cdots\omega_{m_d}\bigr)_{Y_n}\leq
\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}2^{j(d-j)}}{(\omega^d)_X^{d-1}}\bigl(\omega_{m_d}^d\bigr)_{Y_n}\prod_{j=1}^{d-1}\deg_j(f^{k_j}).
\]
Since $\deg_0(f^{k_0})=(\omega^d)_X$ and $\bigl(\omega_{m_d}^d\bigr)_{Y_n}=\deg_d(f^{m_d})=\deg_d(f^{k_d})$, this proves \eqref{eq:volume-gap}.

Now expand $\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})$ and sort its indices as $0\leq m_d\leq\dots\leq m_1\leq n$, with a cost at most $d!$.
By \eqref{eq:volume-gap}, there exists a constant $C_1>0$, independent of $n$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:volume-convolution}
\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})\leq C_1\sum_{\substack{k_0,\ldots,k_d\geq0\\[2pt]k_0+\cdots+k_d=n}}
\prod_{i=0}^d\deg_i(f^{k_i}).
\end{equation}
By \cref{thm:affine-interval-growth} and the definitions of $\Lambda(f)$ and $I_{\max}$, there are constants $C_2>0$ and $q\in(0,1)$ such that, for every $k\geq1$,
\[
\frac{\deg_i(f^k)}{\Lambda(f)^k}\leq
\begin{cases}
C_2k^{2(i-r)(s-i)},&i\in I_{\max},\\
C_2q^k,&i\in \{0,\ldots,d\}\setminus I_{\max}.
\end{cases}
\]
Hence only the indices within $I_{\max}$ contribute to the growth of $\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})/\Lambda(f)^n$.
After summing over the indices $i\in I_{\max}$, it is bounded above by a polynomial in $n$ of degree at most
\[
\ell+\sum_{i=r}^{s}2{(i-r)}(s-i)=\ell+\sum_{j=0}^{\ell}2j(\ell-j)=\frac{\ell^3+2\ell}{3}.
\]
This proves the upper bound in \eqref{eq:volume-growth}.
Finally, by \eqref{eq:standard-exponential-lower-bound}, we have that
\[
\operatorname{vol}(\Gamma_{[n]})\geq \frac{\binom{d}{r}}{d!}\bigl(\omega_{0}^{d-r}\cdot\omega_{n}^{r}\bigr)_{Y_n}=\frac{\deg_r(f^n)}{r!(d-r)!}\geq \frac{\Lambda(f)^n}{r!(d-r)!C_{X,\omega,r}},
\]
so the lower bound in \eqref{eq:volume-growth} follows.

label: cor:generating-series
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:generating-series}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics}, the $i$-th degree generating series
\[
\mathcal{D}_{i,f,\omega}(z)\coloneqq\sum_{n\geq0}\deg_{i,\omega}(f^n)z^n
\]
admits a meromorphic continuation to the disk
\[
|z|<s_i(f)^{-1}=\bigl(\lambda_{i-1}(f)\lambda_{i+1}(f)\bigr)^{-1/2}.
\]
More precisely,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:generating-series}
\mathcal{D}_{i,f,\omega}(z)=\frac{C_{f,\omega,i}}{1-\lambda_i(f)z}+\mathcal{R}_{i,f,\omega}(z),
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{R}_{i,f,\omega}$ is holomorphic on $|z|<s_i(f)^{-1}$.
In particular, $z=\lambda_i(f)^{-1}$ is the unique simple pole in the disk $|z|<s_i(f)^{-1}$, with residue $-C_{f,\omega,i}/\lambda_i(f)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Denote
\[
\mathcal{R}_{i,f,\omega}(z)\coloneqq\sum_{n\geq0}\,\bigl(\deg_{i,\omega}(f^n)-C_{f,\omega,i}\,\lambda_i(f)^n\bigr)z^n.
\]
Since \cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics} holds for every $\eta>s_i(f)$,
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}\left|\deg_{i,\omega}(f^n)-C_{f,\omega,i}\,\lambda_i(f)^n\right|^{1/n}\leq s_i(f).
\]
Hence $\mathcal{R}_{i,f,\omega}$ is holomorphic on the disk $|z|<s_i(f)^{-1}$.
On the original disk of convergence $|z|<\lambda_i(f)^{-1}$ for $\mathcal{D}_{i,f,\omega}(z)$, we have
\[
\mathcal{D}_{i,f,\omega}(z)=C_{f,\omega,i}\sum_{n\geq0}\lambda_i(f)^nz^n+\mathcal{R}_{i,f,\omega}(z)=\frac{C_{f,\omega,i}}{1-\lambda_i(f)z}+\mathcal{R}_{i,f,\omega}(z),
\]
which shows \eqref{eq:generating-series}.
The right-hand side provides the claimed continuation and pole.

label: rmk:BDJ-Nguyen
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:BDJ-Nguyen}
When the characteristic of the ground field $\mathbf{k}$ is not $2$, the meromorphic continuation radius $s_i(f)^{-1}$ in \cref{cor:generating-series} is optimal in every dimension $d\ge2$ and every intermediate codimension.
Indeed, set $d_1\coloneqq 2$ and choose a Bell--Diller--Jonsson surface map $f\colon \mathbb{P}^{d_1}\dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{d_1}$ (e.g., take $\zeta=-3+4\sqrt{-1}$ there), so that
\[
\lambda_1(f) \in \bigl(\sqrt{\lambda_2(f)}, \lambda_2(f)\bigr)\setminus \overline{\mathbf{Q}}.
\]
Thanks to \cite[Corollary~B]{Nguyen26}, the first-degree generating series $\mathcal{D}_{1,f,\mathcal{O}(1)}$ has $|z|=s_1(f)^{-1}=\lambda_2(f)^{-1/2}$ as a natural boundary.

Fix $d\ge2$ and $1\le i\le d-1$.
Set $d_2\coloneqq i-1$ and $d_3\coloneqq d-i-1$.
Choose an integer $q>\lambda_2(f)$.
Let $g_q\colon\mathbb{P}^{d_2}\to\mathbb{P}^{d_2}$ be a $q$-polarized endomorphism and define
\[
F\coloneqq f\times g_q\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb{P}^{d_3}} \colon \mathbb{P}^{d_1}\times\mathbb{P}^{d_2}\times\mathbb{P}^{d_3} \dashrightarrow \mathbb{P}^{d_1}\times\mathbb{P}^{d_2}\times\mathbb{P}^{d_3}.
\]
Using the natural product polarization $H$ on $\mathbb{P}^{d_1}\times\mathbb{P}^{d_2}\times\mathbb{P}^{d_3}$, one can check that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:general-product-degree}
\deg_{k,H}(F^n)=
\sum_{\substack{k_1+k_2+k_3=k\\[3pt]
0\leq k_j\leq d_j}}
\binom{k}{k_1,k_2,k_3}\binom{d-k}{k'_1,k'_2,k'_3}\deg_{k_1,\mathcal{O}(1)}(f^n)q^{k_2n}
\end{equation}
for every $1\le k\le d-1$, where $k'_j\coloneqq d_j-k_j$ for $j=1,2,3$.
It follows that
\[
\lambda_{i-1}(F)=q^{i-1},\qquad
\lambda_i(F)=q^{i-1}\lambda_1(f),\qquad
\lambda_{i+1}(F)=q^{i-1}\lambda_2(f),
\]
and hence
\[
s_i(F)=\sqrt{\lambda_{i-1}(F)\lambda_{i+1}(F)}=q^{i-1}\sqrt{\lambda_2(f)} < \lambda_i(F).
\]
Namely, $i$ is a strict dynamical-degree break for $F$, so \cref{cor:generating-series} applies to $F$ and $i$.

Now specializing \eqref{eq:general-product-degree} to $k=i$, the dominant term of $\deg_{i,H}(F^n)$, corresponding to $(k_1,k_2,k_3)=(1,i-1,0)$, is
\[
i(d-i)q^{(i-1)n}\deg_{1,\mathcal{O}(1)}(f^n).
\]
Let $R_n$ be the sum of all remaining terms, where each one is $O\bigl(q^{(i-1)n}\bigr)$; in particular,
\[
\limsup_{n\to\infty}R_n^{1/n}\le q^{i-1}<q^{i-1}\sqrt{\lambda_2(f)}=s_i(F).
\]
It follows that the $i$-th degree generating series of $F$ with respect to $H$ has the form
\[
\mathcal{D}_{i,F,H}(z)=i(d-i)\mathcal{D}_{1,f,\mathcal{O}(1)}(q^{i-1}z)+\mathcal{H}(z),
\]
where $\mathcal{H}(z)\coloneqq\sum_{n\geq0}R_nz^n$ is holomorphic on a disk strictly larger than $|z|<s_i(F)^{-1}$.
Therefore, the circle $|z|=s_i(F)^{-1}$ is a natural boundary of $\mathcal{D}_{i,F,H}(z)$.

label: prop:abelian-endpoint-failure
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:abelian-endpoint-failure}
Let $E$ be an elliptic curve over $\mathbf{k}$, let $d\geq3$, and let
\[
\Theta\coloneqq \sum_{j=1}^d\operatorname{pr}_j^*[0]
\]
be the product principal polarization on $E^d$, where $\operatorname{pr}_j\colon E^d\to E$ denotes the $j$-th projection.
For every $1\leq i\leq d-1$, there is an isogeny $f=f_{d,i}\colon E^d\to E^d$ such that
\[
\lambda_{i-1}(f)=9^{i-1},\qquad
\lambda_i(f)=9^i,\qquad
\lambda_{i+1}(f)=4\cdot9^i.
\]
In particular, $s_i(f)=6\cdot9^{i-1}<\lambda_i(f)$.
Moreover, for some $c_{d,i}>0$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abelian-endpoint-asymptotic}
\deg_{i,\Theta}(f^n)=3i!(d-i)!\lambda_i(f)^n-c_{d,i}\,n s_i(f)^n+O\bigl(s_i(f)^n\bigr).
\end{equation}
Consequently, the constant $C_{f,\Theta,i}$ in \cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics} equals $3i!(d-i)!$, and
\[
\deg_{i,\Theta}(f^n)-C_{f,\Theta,i}\,\lambda_i(f)^n\sim -c_{d,i}\,n s_i(f)^n.
\]

label: claim:degrees-matrix-norm
title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\[
B_1\coloneqq
\begin{pmatrix}
3&1&0\\
0&2&1\\
0&0&2
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B_2\coloneqq
\begin{pmatrix}
3&1&0\\
0&3&1\\
0&0&2
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and let $f=f_{d,i}$ be the isogeny of $E^d$ induced by
\[
M_{d,i}\coloneqq
\begin{cases}
B_1\oplus I_{d-3},&i=1,\\[2mm]
3I_{i-2}\oplus B_2\oplus I_{d-i-1},&2\leq i\leq d-1.
\end{cases}
\]

\begin{claim}\label{claim:degrees-matrix-norm}
For any $M\in \operatorname{M}_d(\mathbf{Z})$ with nonzero determinant, the induced isogeny $f_M$ of $E^d$ satisfies that for every $0\le j\le d$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abelian-matrix-degree}
\deg_{j,\Theta}(f_M^n)=j!(d-j)!\left\|\bigwedge\nolimits^jM^n\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2,
\end{equation}
where $\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}$ denotes the Frobenius norm of matrices.
In particular,
\[
\lambda_j(f_M)=\rho\Bigl(\bigwedge\nolimits^jM\Bigr)^2.
\]
\end{claim}

\begin{proof}[Proof of Claim \ref{claim:degrees-matrix-norm}]
Under the product principal polarization $\Theta$, $(f_M^n)^*\Theta$ corresponds to the symmetric matrix $(M^n)^{\mathsf{T}}M^n$.
Therefore, for every integer $t\geq0$, the polarization $\Theta+t (f_M^n)^*\Theta$ corresponds to
\[
I_d+t(M^n)^{\mathsf{T}}M^n.
\]
By the Riemann--Roch theorem for abelian varieties \cite[\S16]{Mumford} and the fact that $\deg(f_{M'})=(\det M')^2$ for any $M'\in\operatorname{M}_d(\mathbf{Z})$, we obtain
\[
\frac{1}{d!}\Bigl(\Theta+t\,(f_M^n)^*\Theta\Bigr)^d=\det\Bigl(I_d+t\,(M^n)^{\mathsf{T}}M^n\Bigr).
\]
Expanding both sides yields
\[
\sum_{j=0}^d\frac{\deg_{j,\Theta}(f_M^n)}{j!(d-j)!}\,t^j=\sum_{j=0}^d\operatorname{tr}\Bigl(\bigwedge\nolimits^j\bigl((M^n)^{\mathsf{T}}M^n\bigr)\Bigr)\,t^j.
\]
By functoriality of exterior powers,
\[
\bigwedge\nolimits^j\bigl((M^n)^{\mathsf{T}}M^n\bigr)=\bigwedge\nolimits^j (M^n)^{\mathsf{T}}\bigwedge\nolimits^j M^n=\Bigl(\bigwedge\nolimits^j M^n\Bigr)^{\mathsf{T}}\bigwedge\nolimits^j M^n,
\]
its trace is $\bigl\|\bigwedge^j M^n\bigr\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2$.
Comparing coefficients thus proves \eqref{eq:abelian-matrix-degree}.
The argument is algebraic and remains valid in arbitrary characteristic; see also \cite{Hu24,Hu-GK-AV}.
\end{proof}

We continue with the proof of \cref{prop:abelian-endpoint-failure}.
For every $1\le i\le d-1$, applying \cref{claim:degrees-matrix-norm} with $M=M_{d,i}$, whose $i+1$ eigenvalues of largest modulus are $\underbrace{3,\ldots,3}_{i\text{ copies}},2$, we have
\[
\lambda_{i-1}(f)=9^{i-1},\qquad
\lambda_i(f)=9^i,\qquad
\lambda_{i+1}(f)=4\cdot9^i,
\]
and hence $s_i(f)=6\cdot9^{i-1}<\lambda_i(f)$.

For $i=1$, a direct computation gives
\[
B_1^n=
\begin{pmatrix}
3^n&3^n-2^n&3^n-(n+2)2^{n-1}\\
0&2^n&n2^{n-1}\\
0&0&2^n
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\bigl\|B_1^n\bigr\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2=3\cdot9^n-(n+4)6^n+\frac{n^2+2n+8}{2}\,4^n.
\]
The identity block contributes only $d-3$, so
\[
\bigl\|M_{d,1}^n\bigr\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2=3\cdot9^n-n6^n+O(6^n).
\]

Now assume that $i\geq2$.
The second compound matrix of $B_2$ is
\[
\bigwedge\nolimits^2B_2=
\begin{pmatrix}
9&3&1\\
0&6&2\\
0&0&6
\end{pmatrix},
\]
and hence
\[
\bigwedge\nolimits^2B_2^n=
\begin{pmatrix}
9^n&9^n-6^n&9^n-(n/3+1)6^n\\
0&6^n&(n/3)6^n\\
0&0&6^n
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It follows that
\begin{align*}
\left\|\bigwedge\nolimits^2B_2^n\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2=3\cdot81^n-\left(\frac{2}{3}n+4\right)54^n+\left(\frac{2}{9}n^2+\frac{2}{3}n+4\right)36^n.
\end{align*}
Under the orthogonal decomposition
\[
\bigwedge\nolimits^i\bigl(\mathbf{R}^{i-2}\oplus\mathbf{R}^3\oplus\mathbf{R}^{d-i-1}\bigr)=
\bigoplus_{i_1+i_2+i_3=i}\bigwedge\nolimits^{i_1}\mathbf{R}^{i-2}\otimes\bigwedge\nolimits^{i_2}\mathbf{R}^3\otimes\bigwedge\nolimits^{i_3}\mathbf{R}^{d-i-1},
\]
the summand in $\bigwedge\nolimits^iM_{d,i}^n$ corresponding to $(i_1,i_2,i_3)=(i-2,2,0)$ contributes
\[
9^{(i-2)n}\left\|\bigwedge\nolimits^2B_2^n\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2
\]
to its squared Frobenius norm.
Every other summand has squared spectral radius at most $4\cdot9^{i-1}$, which is strictly smaller than $s_i(f)=6\cdot9^{i-1}$.
The polynomial factors arising from Jordan blocks are therefore absorbed by $O\bigl(s_i(f)^n\bigr)$.
Hence
\[
\left\|\bigwedge\nolimits^iM_{d,i}^n\right\|_{\mathrm{F}}^2=3(9^i)^n-\frac{2}{3}n\bigl(6\cdot9^{i-1}\bigr)^n+O\bigl(s_i(f)^n\bigr).
\]

Finally, applying \cref{claim:degrees-matrix-norm}, we prove \eqref{eq:abelian-endpoint-asymptotic} with $C_{f,\Theta,i}=3i!(d-i)!$ and
\[
c_{d,i}=
\begin{cases}
(d-1)!,&i=1,\\[1mm]
\displaystyle\frac{2}{3}i!(d-i)!,&i\geq2.
\end{cases}
\]
The remaining assertions of \cref{prop:abelian-endpoint-failure} follow readily.

label: cor:surface-endpoint
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:surface-endpoint}
Assume that either \cref{setting:projective} or \cref{setting:kahler} holds, and $d=2$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\arabic*)}]
\item \label{cor:surface-endpoint-strict-break}
If $\lambda_1(f)^2>\lambda_2(f)$, then
\[
\deg_{1,\omega}(f^n)=C_{f,\omega,1}\,\lambda_1(f)^n+O\bigl(\lambda_2(f)^{n/2}\bigr).
\]
\item \label{cor:surface-endpoint-resonant}
If $\lambda_1(f)^2=\lambda_2(f)$, then there is $C>0$ such that for every $n\geq1$,
\[
\operatorname{vol}_X(\omega)\lambda_1(f)^n\leq\deg_{1,\omega}(f^n)\leq Cn^2\lambda_1(f)^n.
\]
\end{enumerate}

title: Proof
body_md:
Note that for every $n\geq1$, $\deg_{0,\omega}(f^n)=\operatorname{vol}_X(\omega)$ and
\[
\deg_{2,\omega}(f^n)=\operatorname{vol}_X(\omega)\lambda_2(f)^n.
\]
It follows that $s_1(f)=\sqrt{\lambda_2(f)}$ and
\[
\sqrt{\deg_{0,\omega}(f^n)\deg_{2,\omega}(f^n)}=\operatorname{vol}_X(\omega)s_1(f)^n.
\]

If $\lambda_1(f)^2>\lambda_2(f)$, then $i=1$ is a strict dynamical-degree break for $f$.
Part~(1) thus follows from \cref{lemma:endpoint-criterion}.
Now assume $\lambda_1(f)^2=\lambda_2(f)$, i.e., $s_1(f)=\lambda_1(f)$.
Then $[0,2]$ is a maximal affine interval, so the upper bound in part~(2) follows from \cref{thm:affine-interval-growth}.
On the other hand, the Khovanskii--Teissier inequality implies
\[
\deg_{1,\omega}(f^n)^2\geq\deg_{0,\omega}(f^n)\deg_{2,\omega}(f^n)=\operatorname{vol}_X(\omega)^2\lambda_1(f)^{2n},
\]
for every $n\geq1$, which proves the stated lower bound.

\label{rmk:polynomial-dyn-deg-known}
Beyond the functorial case just discussed, we record several classes for which all three parts of \cref{question:polynomial-dyn-deg} are known.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\arabic*)}]
\item For \emph{birational} or \emph{bimeromorphic} self-maps of surfaces, the classification of Diller--Favre \cite{DF01} completely settles all three parts: $\mu_1(f)=0$ if $\lambda_1(f)>1$, and $\mu_1(f)\in\{0,1,2\}$ if $\lambda_1(f)=1$; see also \cite[Remark~1.2]{Oguiso16}.

\item Favre--Jonsson \cite[Theorem~C]{FJ11} proved that if $f$ is a dominant polynomial self-map of $\mathbf{C}^2$ satisfying $\lambda_2(f)=\lambda_1(f)^2$, then either the polynomial degree $\deg(f^n)\asymp\lambda_1(f)^n$ or $\deg(f^n)\asymp n\lambda_1(f)^n$; in particular, $\mu_1(f)\in\{0,1\}$.

\item Monomial maps $f\colon\mathbb{P}^d\dashrightarrow\mathbb{P}^d$ induced by matrices $M\in\operatorname{M}_d(\mathbf{Z})$ with $\det M\neq0$ form another class for which all three parts have affirmative answers in every codimension; see \cite[Proposition~4.4]{Lin12b} or \cite[Theorem~A]{FW12}.

\item At every strict dynamical-degree break $\lambda_i(f)>s_i(f)$, \cref{thm:strict-break-asymptotics} shows that for every $s_i(f)<\eta<\lambda_i(f)$,
\[
\deg_{i,\omega}(f^n)=C_{f,\omega,i}\,\lambda_i(f)^n+O(\eta^n).
\]
Thus all three parts hold with $\mu_i(f)=0$.
The surface case was proved by Boucksom--Favre--Jonsson \cite[Main Theorem]{BFJ08}, and the codimension-one case in characteristic zero by Dang--Favre \cite[Theorem~1]{DF21}.
\end{enumerate}

Consequently, the remaining general problem is confined to resonant indices
\[
\lambda_i(f)^2=\lambda_{i-1}(f)\lambda_{i+1}(f).
\]
